project.title: 面向飞机 B-Rep 模型小特征处理的可追溯图学习与几何重建框架
project.target_venue: Journal of Computational Design and Engineering (provisional)

authority_sources.details: Windows 10 Pro 25H2; Intel Core i7-14700KF; NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4060 8 GB (driver 591.86); Python 3.10.20; OpenCASCADE 7.9.0; PyTorch 2.12.1+cu130; fast-simplification 0.2.0. This is a local execution probe, not a substitute for a release manifest.

contract.gap: Existing CAD feature-recognition work provides limited evidence for traceable, risk-sensitive small-feature recognition and downstream geometry processing on complete heterogeneous aircraft B-Rep models.
contract.task: Recognize rivets and surface-features at B-Rep face level, preserve face identifier traceability, and use predictions as candidate inputs to staged CAD processing.
outcomes: per-aircraft error and background false-positive analysis
paired surface-mesh scale and timing comparison

questions.text: Can face geometry and adjacency topology support rivet and surface-feature recognition across complete aircraft models?
Can predictions remain traceable to original or intermediate B-Rep faces and support staged CAD-processing candidates?

contract.contribution: A traceable face-level graph-learning framework that links small-feature predictions on complete-aircraft B-Rep models to staged CAD-processing candidates and paired mesh comparisons.
nonclaims: No universal generalization claim across all aircraft or CAD sources.
Geometric comparison does not establish physics equivalence.
No CAE acceleration or response-preservation claim before controlled downstream experiments.
No mesh-quality or geometric-fidelity superiority claim over QEM.
Human visual review is not described as fully automatic validation.
Retired BFS and 51-dimensional experiments are not part of the formal model.

semantic_locks.canonical: background=0, rivet=1, surface_feature=2; decal and window provenance remains in JSON
Dataset partitioning is performed by complete aircraft model, not by randomly splitting faces
The rivet-stage guard rejects predicted rivet faces with relative area greater than 5e-6; no corresponding global area threshold is applied to the surface-feature branch.

terminology.concept: surface target class in manuscript prose

style_profile.language_variant: British English for manuscript; Simplified Chinese for planning

facts.value: 48 node features, 6 edge attributes, 4 layers, hidden dimension 64, seed 123, 50 epochs, rivet threshold 0.9, surface threshold 0.5

alignment.method: B-Rep face graph with geometric and topological attributes
alignment.evidence: Complete-aircraft test evaluation, per-aircraft target-class counts and F1, and background false-positive risk
alignment.result: Across 34162 test faces from nine aircraft, rivet F1=0.9312 and surface-feature F1=0.8091; 28 rivet and 122 surface-feature faces were missed in total, including 103 surface-feature faces on Airbus; Air Plane Idea A contributes 82 of 190 background false positives
alignment.interpretation: Face-level recognition is feasible in the reported partition, but pooled metrics do not establish uniform target-class performance across aircraft and residual background false-positive risk remains relevant to downstream processing
alignment.limitation: Some test aircraft may have been used during historical development; limited aircraft and CAD-source diversity

alignment.method: face identifier traceability, CAD removal, and local reconstruction
alignment.evidence: Face-identifier alignment between original-model recognition and CAD-input predictions, nine original--simplified B-Rep pairs, fixed OpenCASCADE meshing controls, and a matched-triangle QEM timing-component baseline
alignment.result: Across the nine pairs, triangle reduction was 0.57--48.66 percent and median meshing-time reduction was 2.49--58.29 percent. At matched triangle targets, final meshing was 7.22--60.05 percent lower than original meshing plus the QEM kernel under the stated limited timing account.
alignment.interpretation: Original-model predictions align face by face across recognition and CAD-input records; the added planar-patch check accounts for the rivet-count difference. The reported pairs have reduced mesh scale and meshing time under the tested controls, without establishing removal completeness, end-to-end superiority, mesh-quality superiority, or engineering-response equivalence.
alignment.limitation: Candidate records do not establish operation-level outcomes; matched-quality QEM comparison and downstream CAE evidence remain unavailable.
alignment.contribution: Traceable downstream CAD-processing candidates and paired mesh comparison

required_fields: paired mesh node and triangle counts

decisions.decision: Plan the paper as an end-to-end recognition and geometry-processing framework, with a recognition-only fallback title if downstream evidence remains insufficient.
Treat the 3631-face evaluation as historical because it does not match the current 34156-face candidate test CSV.
By author instruction, describe the study in terms of B-Rep models and face identifier traceability, without presenting STEP as a file-format contribution.
By author confirmation, use the current 17-aircraft training and 9-aircraft test partition as the fixed evaluation dataset; the earlier dataset-scope mismatch is resolved.

By author instruction, organize related work from three-dimensional scene segmentation to CAD feature recognition, then state the bounded gap for learning-guided small-geometry processing in industrial simulation workflows; do not claim mesh or simulation effects without controlled evidence.

By author instruction, introduce concise B-Rep preliminaries before the learning formulation, treat small geometry only as a supervised label contract, and make face-graph encoding and dual-specialist graph learning the theoretical focus of Section 3.

By author instruction, present Chapter 4 as a concise traceable processing contract: retain candidate filtering principles, staged face identifier handling, and operation alternatives, but do not enumerate detailed boundary-case rules or legal-status checks in the main text.

By author instruction, organise the experimental evidence into training and face-level recognition (6.1), CAD simplification with original--simplified surface-mesh comparison (6.2), and cross-aircraft variation with evidence boundaries (6.3); do not fabricate a training-convergence curve when epoch-wise records are unavailable.

For the current integration revision, report the observed recognition and surface-mesh results in the abstract and conclusion, and describe the fixed nine-aircraft partition as developmental because historical use of some test aircraft remains possible.
